# CLI Feature Guide: Visualizations & In-Line Charts

[← Back to CLI Reference Hub](../cli.md)

`pytae` includes first-class visualization capabilities directly from the command line:
- **Terminal In-Line Visualizations**: Instant ASCII frequency bars (`-freq`) and numeric distribution histograms (`-hist`) rendered directly in console scrollback.
- **Headless Figure Plotting**: Full Matplotlib publication-grade plotting via `-plot` and `-finalize`, with automatic figure export (`-o plot.png`).

---

## Contents

- [Overview & Quick Reference](#overview--quick-reference)
- [Terminal Frequency Distribution (`-freq`)](#terminal-frequency-distribution--freq)
- [Terminal Numeric Histograms (`-hist`)](#terminal-numeric-histograms--hist)
- [Headless Figure Plotting (`-plot` & `-finalize`)](#headless-figure-plotting--plot--finalize)
  - [1. Single Plots with Explicit Pipeline Aggregation](#1-single-plots-with-explicit-pipeline-aggregation)
  - [2. Multi-Dimensional Categorical Grouping (`by=`)](#2-multi-dimensional-categorical-grouping-by)
  - [3. Distribution Plots (`box`, `kde`, `hist`)](#3-distribution-plots-box-kde-hist)
  - [4. Custom Styling & Finalization (`-finalize`)](#4-custom-styling--finalization--finalize)
  - [5. Exporting Figures (`-o`)](#5-exporting-figures--o)
- [Interactive Viewing](#interactive-viewing)

---

## Overview & Quick Reference

| Flag | Category | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-freq COL` | Terminal ASCII | Categorical distribution bar chart | `pytae penguins.parquet -freq species` |
| `-hist COL[:BINS]` | Terminal ASCII | Numeric binned distribution histogram | `pytae penguins.parquet -hist body_mass_g:8` |
| `-plot SPEC` | Figure Plot | Draw bar, line, scatter, box, area, kde | `pytae data.csv -plot "kind=bar,x=cat,y=val"` |
| `-finalize SPEC` | Figure Style | Title, axis labels, styles, tight layout | `pytae data.csv -finalize "title='Sales',style=dark_background"` |
| `-o TARGET.ext` | Export | Save figure to PNG, SVG, PDF, etc. | `-o chart.png -out_dir ./figures` |

---

## Terminal Frequency Distribution (`-freq`)

Render instant ASCII horizontal bars with exact counts and percentages for any categorical column:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -freq species
```

**Output:**
```text
species    count
Adelie       152  ████████████████████ (44.2%)
Gentoo       124  ████████████████     (36.0%)
Chinstrap     68  █████████            (19.8%)
```

Respects `-dropna` (excludes missing categories from the count and distribution):
```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -dropna sex -freq sex
```

**Output:**
```text
   sex  Count                 Distribution
  Male    168 ████████████████████ (50.5%)
Female    165 ████████████████████ (49.5%)
```

---

## Terminal Numeric Histograms (`-hist`)

Inspect numeric distributions, spreads, and peaks directly in your console:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -hist body_mass_g:6
```

**Output:**
```text
body_mass_g            count
[2700.0, 3300.0)          63  ████████████
[3300.0, 3900.0)         105  ████████████████████
[3900.0, 4500.0)          69  █████████████
[4500.0, 5100.0)          57  ███████████
[5100.0, 5700.0)          40  ████████
[5700.0, 6300.0]           8  ██
```

- If bins count is omitted (`-hist body_mass_g`), defaults to 10 bins.
- Automatically handles missing values and filters out non-numeric rows.

---

## Headless Figure Plotting (`-plot` & `-finalize`)

`-plot` connects `pytae`'s visualization engine (`Plotter`) directly to the command line. Any pipeline can end with a plot and route directly to disk or interactive screen.

### 1. Single Plots with Explicit Pipeline Aggregation

Filter, aggregate, and plot in one pipeline:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet \
  -by species \
  -agg "avg_mass=body_mass_g:mean" \
  -plot "kind=bar, x=species, y=avg_mass" \
  -finalize "title='Average Body Mass by Species', ylabel='Mass (g)'" \
  -o avg_mass.png
```

### 2. Multi-Dimensional Categorical Grouping (`by=`)

Produce multi-series bar or scatter plots with automated color mapping:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet \
  -filter "sex = ('notna',)" \
  -plot "kind=scatter, x=bill_length_mm, y=body_mass_g, by=species" \
  -finalize "title='Bill Length vs Body Mass', tight_layout=true" \
  -o scatter.png
```

### 3. Distribution Plots (`box`, `kde`, `hist`)

Visualise unaggregated distributions grouped by category:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet \
  -plot "kind=box, x=species, y=flipper_length_mm" \
  -finalize "title='Flipper Length Distribution by Species'" \
  -o flipper_box.png
```

### 4. Custom Styling & Finalization (`-finalize`)

Pass any figure-level customization keys to `-finalize`:

```bash
pytae tips.parquet \
  -by day -agg "avg_bill=total_bill:mean" \
  -plot "kind=bar, x=day, y=avg_bill" \
  -finalize "title='Average Bill by Day', style=seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid, xlabel='Day of Week', ylabel='Average Bill ($)'" \
  -o daily_bill.svg
```

Supported `-finalize` keys:
- `title='...'`: Figure or chart title
- `xlabel='...'`, `ylabel='...'`: Axis labels
- `style='...'`: Matplotlib style sheet (e.g. `seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid`, `dark_background`)
- `tight_layout=true`: Apply tight bounding box
- `sharex=true`, `sharey=true`: Link axis scales across subplots

### 5. Exporting Figures (`-o`)

When `-o` specifies an image extension (`.png`, `.svg`, `.pdf`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`), `pytae` automatically switches to the non-interactive Matplotlib backend (`Agg`) and saves the figure directly to the destination:

```bash
# Save to current working directory
pytae data.parquet -plot "kind=bar,x=cat,y=val" -o chart.png

# Save to dedicated output directory (created automatically if missing)
pytae data.parquet -plot "kind=bar,x=cat,y=val" -o chart.png -od ./reports/figures
```

---

## Interactive Viewing

If `-o` is omitted and the output is not redirected, `pytae` invokes `plt.show()` so you can inspect charts interactively in a desktop window:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -plot "kind=scatter, x=bill_length_mm, y=body_mass_g, by=species"
```

# FILE: docs/cli/reshape.md
################################################################################
# CLI Feature Guide: Reshaping (Pure 1-to-1: `-long` & `-wide`)

[← Back to CLI Reference Hub](../cli.md)

Pure structural 1-to-1 reshaping between long and wide formats without aggregation.

---

## Contents

- [Overview & Quick Reference](#overview--quick-reference)
- [Unpivoting Wide to Long (`-long`)](#unpivoting-wide-to-long--long)
- [Pivoting Long to Wide (`-wide`)](#pivoting-long-to-wide--wide)
  - [1. Pure 1-to-1 Unmelting](#1-pure-1-to-1-unmelting)
  - [2. Explicit Row Index (`r=`)](#2-explicit-row-index-r)
  - [3. Round-Trip Reshaping (`-long` → `-wide`)](#3-round-trip-reshaping--long---wide)
- [When to Use `-pivot` Instead of `-wide`](#when-to-use--pivot-instead-of--wide)

---

## Overview & Quick Reference

`-long` and `-wide` are designed as a **strictly complementary, 1-to-1 reshaping pair**:

| Flag | Description | Key Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `-long [SPEC]` | Melt numeric columns into rows | `cols=` (columns to melt), `id_vars=` (fixed rows), `c=` (metric header), `v=` (value header) |
| `-wide [SPEC]` | Pure 1-to-1 reshape: spread long rows into headers | `r=` (row index), `c=` (header source), `v=` (values) |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **`-wide` is strictly for 1-to-1 reshaping without aggregation.** If your data has multiple rows per key combination and requires mathematical summarization (`mean`, `sum`, `count`/`n`), use **[`-pivot`](pivot.md)**.
> For row deduplication, see **[`-distinct`](distinct.md)**; for sorting rows, see **[`-arrange`](arrange.md)**.

---

## Unpivoting Wide to Long (`-long`)

Melts all numeric columns into row-wise key-value pairs (`variable` and `value`), keeping non-numeric identifier columns intact:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet \
  -select "species,bill_length_mm,bill_depth_mm" \
  -long \
  -head 4
```

**Output:**

| species   | variable       |   value |
|:----------|:---------------|--------:|
| Adelie    | bill_length_mm |    39.1 |
| Adelie    | bill_length_mm |    39.5 |
| Adelie    | bill_length_mm |    40.3 |
| Adelie    | bill_length_mm |   nan   |

Customize column names with `c=` and `v=`:
```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -long "c=metric,v=measurement" -head 4
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    | sex    | metric         |   measurement |
|:----------|:----------|:-------|:---------------|--------------:|
| Adelie    | Torgersen | Male   | bill_length_mm |          39.1 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen | Female | bill_length_mm |          39.5 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen | Female | bill_length_mm |          40.3 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen | nan    | bill_length_mm |         nan   |

---

## Pivoting Long to Wide (`-wide`)

`-wide` performs pure structural un-melting (inverse of `-long`), pivoting values from column `c=` into separate column headers using values from `v=`.

### 1. Pure 1-to-1 Unmelting

Given a long dataset with unique row keys (such as `flights.parquet` with unique `year` + `month` pairs):

```bash
pytae flights.parquet -wide "c=month,v=passengers" -head 3
```

**Output:**

|   year |   Jan |   Feb |   Mar |   Apr |   May |   Jun |   Jul |   Aug |   Sep |   Oct |   Nov |   Dec |
|-------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|
|   1949 |   112 |   118 |   132 |   129 |   121 |   135 |   148 |   148 |   136 |   119 |   104 |   118 |
|   1950 |   115 |   126 |   141 |   135 |   125 |   149 |   170 |   170 |   158 |   133 |   114 |   140 |
|   1951 |   145 |   150 |   178 |   163 |   172 |   178 |   199 |   199 |   184 |   162 |   146 |   166 |

### 2. Explicit Row Index (`r=`)

By default, all columns other than `c` and `v` serve as row identifiers. Use `r=` to declare specific row index columns explicitly:

```bash
pytae flights.parquet -wide "r=year,c=month,v=passengers" -head 3
```

**Output:**

|   year |   Jan |   Feb |   Mar |   Apr |   May |   Jun |   Jul |   Aug |   Sep |   Oct |   Nov |   Dec |
|-------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|------:|
|   1949 |   112 |   118 |   132 |   129 |   121 |   135 |   148 |   148 |   136 |   119 |   104 |   118 |
|   1950 |   115 |   126 |   141 |   135 |   125 |   149 |   170 |   170 |   158 |   133 |   114 |   140 |
|   1951 |   145 |   150 |   178 |   163 |   172 |   178 |   199 |   199 |   184 |   162 |   146 |   166 |

### 3. Round-Trip Reshaping (`-long` → `-wide`)

Because `-long` and `-wide` are strict 1-to-1 bijections, you can melt and immediately un-melt back to the original tabular structure:

```bash
pytae items.parquet \
  -long "c=variable,v=value" \
  -wide "c=variable,v=value"
```

**Output:**

| id | val1 | val2 |
|:---|---:|---:|
| row1 | 10.0 | 100.0 |
| row2 | 20.0 | 200.0 |
| row3 | 30.0 | 300.0 |

---

## When to Use `-pivot` Instead of `-wide`

| Scenario | Use `-wide` | Use `-pivot` |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Unique key-value pairs (1:1 un-melting)** | ✅ Yes | Optional |
| **Duplicate key-value combinations** | ❌ Raises error | ✅ Yes (aggregates) |
| **Mathematical summaries (`sum`, `mean`, etc.)** | ❌ Not supported | ✅ Yes (`a=sum`, `a=mean`) |
| **Two-way frequency counts (`a=n`)** | ❌ Not supported | ✅ Yes (`a=n`) |
| **Fill empty cells (`f_v=0`)** | ❌ (leaves `NaN`) | ✅ Yes (`f_v=0`) |

If duplicate keys are passed to `-wide`, `pytae` stops immediately and directs you to `-pivot`:

```text
pytae: error: wide() encountered duplicate entries for index [...] and column '...'. wide() is strictly for 1-to-1 reshaping without aggregation. Use pt.pivot() / -pivot to summarize or aggregate duplicate entries.
```

👉 See the complete **[2D Pivot Tables Guide](pivot.md)** for all multi-dimensional aggregation patterns.

# CLI Feature Guide: Column Selection

[← Back to CLI Reference Hub](../cli.md)

Select, filter, reorder, and exclude columns using names, negative prefixes, ranges, pattern matching, or data types with `-select`.

---

## Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Selecting Explicit Columns](#selecting-explicit-columns)
- [Negative Selection & Exclusion (`-col`, `~col`, `exclude=`)](#negative-selection--exclusion)
- [Slice Notation (`start:end`)](#slice-notation-startend)
- [Pattern Matching (`contains=`, `startswith=`, `endswith=`, `regex=`)](#pattern-matching)
- [Data Type Filtering (`dtype=`, `exclude_dtype=`)](#data-type-filtering)
- [Chaining `-select` in Pipelines](#chaining--select-in-pipelines)

---

## Overview

`-select` provides unified column management across the entire CLI pipeline, matching the Python library's `pt.select()` verb.

| Capability | Syntax / Flag | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Explicit names | `col1,col2` | `-select "species,island,body_mass_g"` |
| Negative selection | `-col` or `~col` | `-select "-species"` or `-select "~island"` |
| Negative slices | `-start:end` | `-select "-bill_length_mm:flipper_length_mm"` |
| Keyword exclusion | `exclude=col` | `-select "exclude=species"` |
| Column slice | `start:end` | `-select "bill_length_mm:body_mass_g"` |
| Substring / prefix / suffix | `contains=`, `startswith=`, `endswith=` | `-select "contains=bill"` |
| Regular expression | `regex=PATTERN` | `-select "regex=^bill_.*mm$"` |
| Data type filter | `dtype=numeric` / `exclude_dtype=category` | `-select "dtype=numeric"` |

---

## Selecting Explicit Columns

List column names separated by commas. The output DataFrame columns are ordered exactly as listed in the `-select` argument:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "species,island,body_mass_g" -head 3
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|:----------|--------------:|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          3750 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          3800 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          3250 |

Reorder columns on the fly:
```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "body_mass_g,species" -head 3
```

**Output:**

|   body_mass_g | species   |
|--------------:|:----------|
|          3750 | Adelie    |
|          3800 | Adelie    |
|          3250 | Adelie    |

---

<a id="negative-selection--exclusion"></a>
## Negative Selection & Exclusion (`-col`, `~col`, `exclude=`)

You can exclude specific columns, combinations, or slices directly within `-select`. Remaining columns preserve their original relative order.

### Negated Column Names (`-col` or `~col`)

Prefix a column name with `-` or `~` to exclude it:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "-species" -head 3
```

**Output:**

| island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |

Multiple negated columns can be combined in quotes:
```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "-species, -island, -sex" -head 3
```

**Output:**

|   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g |
|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|
|             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 |
|             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 |
|             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 |

### Negated Slices (`-start:end`)

Exclude a contiguous range of columns:
```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "-bill_length_mm:flipper_length_mm" -head 3
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|:----------|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          3800 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          3250 | Female |

### Keyword Exclusion (`exclude=`)

Use the `exclude=` parameter to exclude one or more columns:
```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "exclude=species" -head 3
```

**Output:**

| island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |

---

## Slice Notation (`start:end`)

Select a contiguous range of columns from `start` up to and including `end` (using pandas column position order):

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "bill_length_mm:body_mass_g" -head 3
```

**Output:**

|   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g |
|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|
|             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 |
|             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 |
|             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 |

---

## Pattern Matching

Match column names dynamically without typing every name:

| Token | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `contains=TEXT` | Column names containing `TEXT` | `contains=bill` |
| `startswith=PREFIX` | Column names starting with `PREFIX` | `startswith=bill_` |
| `endswith=SUFFIX` | Column names ending with `SUFFIX` | `endswith=_mm` |
| `regex=PATTERN` | Column names matching regular expression | `regex=^bill_.*mm$` |

### Example: Contains

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "contains=bill" -head 3
```

**Output:**

|   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |
|-----------------:|----------------:|
|             39.1 |            18.7 |
|             39.5 |            17.4 |
|             40.3 |            18   |

### Combining names with pattern tokens

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "species,contains=bill" -head 3
```

**Output:**

| species   |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |
|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|
| Adelie    |             39.1 |            18.7 |
| Adelie    |             39.5 |            17.4 |
| Adelie    |             40.3 |            18   |

---

## Data Type Filtering

Select or exclude columns by data type:

| Token | Description |
|---|---|
| `dtype=numeric` | Numeric columns (`int64`, `float64`, etc.) |
| `dtype=object` / `dtype=str` | String or object columns |
| `dtype=datetime` | Datetime / timestamp columns |
| `exclude_dtype=category` | Exclude categorical columns |

### Example: Numeric Only

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -select "dtype=numeric" -head 3
```

**Output:**

|   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g |
|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|
|             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 |
|             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 |
|             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 |

---

## Chaining `-select` in Pipelines

`-select` can be repeated across intermediate pipeline steps (e.g. after `-mutate` or `-agg`), or chained sequentially to filter then subtract:

```bash
# Select numeric columns, then subtract bill_depth_mm
pytae penguins.parquet -select "dtype=numeric" -select "-bill_depth_mm" -head 3
```

**Output:**

|   bill_length_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g |
|-----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|
|             39.1 |                 181 |          3750 |
|             39.5 |                 186 |          3800 |
|             40.3 |                 195 |          3250 |

```bash
# Narrowing output columns after an aggregation
pytae penguins.parquet \
  -by species \
  -agg "avg_mass = body_mass_g:mean, total = n" \
  -select "species,avg_mass"
```

**Output:**

| species   |   avg_mass |
|:----------|-----------:|
| Adelie    |    3700.66 |
| Chinstrap |    3733.09 |
| Gentoo    |    5076.02 |

# CLI Feature Guide: SQL Engine

[← Back to CLI Reference Hub](../cli.md)

Execute full analytical SQL queries directly against tabular files and in-memory pipeline views via Polars SQLContext using `-sql`.

---

## Contents

- [Overview & Architecture](#overview--architecture)
- [Basic Queries Against Table `data`](#basic-queries-against-table-data)
- [Aggregations & Grouping](#aggregations--grouping)
- [Window Functions](#window-functions)
- [Common Table Expressions (CTEs)](#common-table-expressions-ctes)
- [Columns With Spaces & Identifier Quoting](#columns-with-spaces--identifier-quoting)
- [Reading SQL From File (`@query.sql`)](#reading-sql-from-file-querysql)
- [Multi-File SQL Joins](#multi-file-sql-joins)

---

## Overview & Architecture

Pytae integrates the native Polars SQL engine (`SQLContext`) to provide zero-copy, vectorized SQL execution directly against your data without external dependencies:
- In single-file pipelines, the current dataset view is queryable as table **`data`**.
- In multi-file mode (`-file`), each file alias (e.g. `df1`, `df2`) is queryable directly by name.
- SQL can be inserted at any point in the pipeline and chained with other pytae flags.

---

## Basic Queries Against Table `data`

Filter and select columns with standard SQL syntax:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -sql "select species, island, body_mass_g from data where body_mass_g > 5500" -head 3
```

**Output:**

| species   | island   |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|:---------|--------------:|
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          5700 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          5700 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          5550 |

---

## Aggregations & Grouping

Perform group aggregations, aliases, and ordering:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet \
  -sql "select species, count(*) as count, round(avg(body_mass_g), 1) as avg_mass from data group by species order by avg_mass desc"
```

**Output:**

| species   |   count |   avg_mass |
|:----------|--------:|-----------:|
| Gentoo    |     124 |     5076   |
| Chinstrap |      68 |     3733.1 |
| Adelie    |     152 |     3700.7 |

---

## Window Functions

Run analytical window functions such as `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()`, or running totals:

```bash
# Top 2 heaviest penguins per species
pytae penguins.parquet \
  -sql "select species, body_mass_g, row_number() over (partition by species order by body_mass_g desc) as rnk from data where body_mass_g is not null" \
  -filter "rnk <= 2"
```

**Output:**

| species   |   body_mass_g |   rnk |
|:----------|--------------:|------:|
| Adelie    |          4775 |     1 |
| Adelie    |          4725 |     2 |
| Chinstrap |          4800 |     1 |
| Chinstrap |          4550 |     2 |
| Gentoo    |          6300 |     1 |
| Gentoo    |          6050 |     2 |

---

## Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

Complex multi-step queries with `WITH` clauses work seamlessly:

```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -sql "
  with summary as (
    select species, avg(body_mass_g) as avg_mass
    from data
    where body_mass_g is not null
    group by species
  )
  select * from summary order by avg_mass desc
"
```

**Output:**

| species   |   avg_mass |
|:----------|-----------:|
| Gentoo    |    5076.02 |
| Chinstrap |    3733.09 |
| Adelie    |    3700.66 |

---

## Columns With Spaces & Identifier Quoting

Standard SQL quoting applies:
- Column names with spaces must be escaped with escaped double quotes `\"col a\"` or brackets `[col a]`.
- String literals must use single quotes `'val'`.

```bash
pytae data.parquet -sql "select \"body mass g\", \"bill length mm\" from data where species = 'Adelie'"
```

---

## Reading SQL From File (`@query.sql`)

For long or reusable queries, place the SQL query in a `.sql` file:

```sql
-- analysis.sql
SELECT
    species,
    island,
    COUNT(*) AS total_penguins,
    ROUND(AVG(body_mass_g), 2) AS mean_weight
FROM data
WHERE sex IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY species, island
ORDER BY mean_weight DESC;
```

Execute via:
```bash
pytae penguins.parquet -sql @analysis.sql
```

**Output:**

| species | island | total_penguins | mean_weight |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| Gentoo | Biscoe | 119 | 5092.44 |
| Chinstrap | Dream | 68 | 3733.09 |
| Adelie | Biscoe | 44 | 3709.66 |
| Adelie | Torgersen | 47 | 3708.51 |
| Adelie | Dream | 55 | 3701.36 |

---

## Multi-File SQL Joins

In `-file` mode, combine disparate datasets using standard SQL `JOIN`:

```bash
pytae -file "customers.csv=c; orders.parquet=o" \
  -sql "select c.customer_id, c.name, count(o.order_id) as num_orders, sum(o.amount) as total_spent from c left join o on c.customer_id = o.customer_id group by c.customer_id, c.name order by c.customer_id"
```

**Output:**

| customer_id | name | num_orders | total_spent |
|---:|:---|---:|---:|
| 1 | Alice | 2 | 400.0 |
| 2 | Bob | 1 | 300.0 |
| 3 | Charlie | 0 | NaN |

<a id="calling-paradigms"></a>
## Calling Paradigms: Accessor vs. Function

Every operation in `pytae` is accessible through two equivalent styles:

1. **Accessor Chain (`df.pt.<verb>()`)**: Chains smoothly with standard pandas methods (`.rename()`, `.sort_values()`, `.assign()`). Preferred in interactive notebooks and pipelines.
2. **Function Style (`pt.<verb>(df, ...)`)**: Pure functional form, ideal for standalone transformations and scripts.

```python
import pytae as pt
import pandas as pd

penguins = pt.sample("penguins")

# 1. Accessor chain: seamless integration with pandas
(
    penguins.pt.filter("body_mass_g > 3000, species == 'Gentoo'")
    .pt.select("species", "island", "bill_length_mm", "body_mass_g")
    .pt.mutate(mass_kg="body_mass_g / 1000")
    .pt.arrange("mass_kg desc")
    .pt.by("species", "island")
    .pt.agg(a=["mean", "n"])
)
```

**Output:**

| species | island | n | bill_length_mm | body_mass_g | mass_kg |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Gentoo | Biscoe | 123 | 47.5049 | 5076.02 | 5.07602 |

```python
# 2. Function style: standalone calls
subset = pt.select(penguins, "species", contains="bill")
summary = pt.agg(pt.by(subset, "species"), "mean")
```

---

<a id="functional-areas"></a>
## Functional Areas at a Glance

### 1. Row Filtering — `filter()`

Filter rows using intuitive callables/lambdas, string expressions, python dictionaries, or keyword arguments. Safely handles column names with spaces without awkward escaping:

```python
# Bare callables / lambdas
penguins.pt.filter(lambda d: d["body_mass_g"] > 4000)

# String expressions (handles spaced names directly)
penguins.pt.filter("body_mass_g > 3500, species == 'Adelie'")

# Plain dictionary syntax
df.pt.filter({"bill length mm": "> 40", "island": "Biscoe"})

# Keyword arguments with intervals and string operators
pt.filter(penguins, body_mass_g="[3000, 4500]", species=("startswith", "Ad"))
```

👉 **Complete Guide:** [library/filter.md](library/filter.md)

---

### 2. Column Selection — `select()`

Select, filter, reorder, or exclude columns using exact names, negative prefixes (`-col`, `~col`), negative slices (`-start:end`), keyword exclusion (`exclude=`), regex patterns, or data type categories:

```python
pt.select(penguins, "species", "island")  # Exact column order
pt.select(penguins, "-species")  # Exclude column (negative selection)
pt.select(penguins, "-bill_length_mm:body_mass_g")  # Negative slice
pt.select(penguins, exclude=["species", "island"])  # Keyword exclusion
pt.select(penguins, "species:bill_length_mm")  # Contiguous slice
pt.select(penguins, contains="bill", dtype="numeric")  # Pattern union
pt.select(penguins, exclude_dtype="numeric")  # Invert selection
```

👉 **Complete Guide:** [library/select.md](library/select.md)

---

### 3. Feature Engineering — `mutate()`

Compute new columns or overwrite existing ones using python expressions evaluated in order via pandas `eval()`. Includes built-in functional helpers like `if_else`, `case_when`, `coalesce`, and `map`:

```python
# Formulas and sequential derivation
pt.mutate(penguins, mass_kg="body_mass_g / 1000", mass_lb="mass_kg * 2.20462")

# Functional helpers: if_else, case_when, coalesce, map
pt.mutate(penguins, weight_class="if_else(body_mass_g > 4000, 'heavy', 'light')")
pt.mutate(penguins, tier="case_when((body_mass_g >= 4500, 'large'), (body_mass_g >= 3500, 'medium'), default='small')")
pt.mutate(df, contact="coalesce(mobile, home_phone, work_phone, 'N/A')")
pt.mutate(penguins, code="map(species, {'Adelie': 'A', 'Gentoo': 'G'}, 'Other')")

# Grouped window calculations without collapsing rows (inherited from standalone pt.by)
pt.mutate(pt.by(penguins, "species"), avg_mass="mean(body_mass_g)", diff="body_mass_g - avg_mass", n="n")

# Multi-column transforms using (col1, col2) and _ placeholder (in-place, suffix/prefix, or selectors)
penguins.pt.mutate("(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) = _ / 10")
penguins.pt.mutate("(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)_cm = _ / 10")
penguins.pt.mutate("(startswith=bill_) = _ / 10")
penguins.pt.by("species").pt.mutate("z_(dtype=numeric) = (_ - mean(_)) / std(_)")

# Control NA grouping with dropna (dropna=False by default calculates on NA group; dropna=True fills NaN)
pt.mutate(pt.by(df, "group"), avg_val="mean(val)", dropna=True)
```

👉 **Complete Guide:** [library/mutate.md](library/mutate.md)

---

### 4. Sorting & Picking Extreme Rows — `arrange()` & `pick()`

Order rows or retrieve the top/bottom records with group awareness:

```python
# Reorder rows: asc, desc, leading minus, and brackets for spaces
pt.arrange(penguins, "species", "body_mass_g desc")
pt.arrange(penguins, "-body_mass_g")
pt.arrange(penguins, "[bill length mm] desc")

# Pick top / bottom records overall or within groups
pt.pick(penguins, "body_mass_g", n=3)  # Top 3 (default order="max")
pt.pick(penguins, "body_mass_g", n=1, order="min")  # Lightest penguin
pt.pick(penguins, "body_mass_g", prop=0.1)  # Top 10%

# Method chaining with group context
(penguins.pt.arrange("species, -body_mass_g").pt.by("species").pt.pick("body_mass_g", n=2))
```

👉 **Complete Guides:** [library/arrange.md](library/arrange.md) (Sorting) • [library/pick.md](library/pick.md) (Picking Rows)

---

### 5. Distinct Rows — Removing Duplicate Rows

Drop duplicate records across the intermediate DataFrame with full control over column subsets, with automatic 0-indexed RangeIndex reset:

```python
# Eliminate duplicates across all selected columns via accessor
penguins.pt.select("species", "island").pt.distinct()

# Restrict uniqueness constraint to specific columns (positional arguments only)
penguins.pt.distinct("species", "island")

# Functional style
pt.distinct(penguins, "species", "island")
```

👉 **Complete Guide:** [library/distinct.md](library/distinct.md)

---

### 6. Pure Reshaping — `long()` & `wide()`

Reshape between long and wide formats using consistent `c=` (column dimension), `v=` (value column), and `r=` (row identifiers) parameter roles:

```python
# Melt numeric columns into (feature, value) rows
tall = pt.long(penguins, c="feature", v="reading")

# Pure reshape: spread long-form records back to columns
wide = pt.wide(tall, c="feature", v="reading")
```

👉 **Complete Guide:** [library/reshape.md](library/reshape.md)

---

### 7. 2D Pivot Tables — `pivot()`

Excel-style 2D pivot table engine with the intuitive `r, c, v, a` vocabulary. Guarantees flat 1D column names and automatically resets index to `RangeIndex(0, 1, 2, ...)`:

```python
# 2D summary grid of mean body mass across island and species
pt.pivot(penguins, r="island", c="species", v="body_mass_g", a="mean")

# Frequency matrix (count rows across dimensions; v can be omitted for row counts)
pt.pivot(penguins, r="island", c="species", a="n")

# Hierarchical multi-row summary
pt.pivot(penguins, r=["island", "sex"], c="species", v="body_mass_g", a="mean", f_v=0)
```

👉 **Complete Guide:** [library/pivot.md](library/pivot.md)

---

### 8. Grouping & Aggregation — `by()`, `ungroup()`, `agg()`

Set grouping context with `.pt.by(*cols)` which flows into subsequent `.pt.mutate()`, `.pt.agg()`, and `.pt.pick()`. Clear grouping at any time using `.pt.ungroup()`. Calling `.pt.agg()` automatically clears the active grouping upon completion:

```python
# Grouped aggregation via pipeline chaining
penguins.pt.by("species", "island").pt.agg("mean")

# Grouped window mutation inheriting active grouping
penguins.pt.by("species").pt.mutate("mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g), diff = body_mass_g - mean_mass")

# Clear grouping explicitly
penguins.pt.by("species").pt.ungroup()

# Direct functional agg
pt.agg(penguins, "species", "mean")  # Mean of all numeric columns per species
pt.agg(penguins, ["species", "island"], ["mean", "sum", "n"])  # Multi-column grouping
pt.agg(penguins, "species", body_mass_g="mean", count="n")  # Column-specific aggregations
pt.agg(
    tips.rename(columns={"total_bill": "total bill"}), "smoker", "tip = mean, [total bill] = mean, n = n"
)  # String spec with bracketed spaced columns
pt.agg(penguins, "species", total="body_mass_g:sum")  # Named aggregation
pt.agg(penguins, None, a=["mean", "n"])  # Whole-table summary (no grouping)
```

👉 **Complete Guide:** [library/agg.md](library/agg.md)

---

<a id="9-plotting--plotter"></a>
### 9. Plotting — `Plotter` & `df.pt.plot()`

Method-chainable visualization engine built on Matplotlib and `pandas.plot()`. Supports automated grouping, secondary Y-axes, complex multi-panel mosaic dashboards, small-multiples grid faceting, and direct accessor chaining via `df.pt.plot()`:

```python
# Direct accessor chaining
(
    penguins.pt.select("species", "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm")
    .pt.plot(kind="scatter", x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", by="species", palette="tab10")
    .finalize()
)

# Multi-panel mosaic dashboard
p = pt.Plotter(penguins, mosaic="AB", figsize=(10, 4))
p.plot(on="A", kind="scatter", x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", by="species")
p.plot(on="B", kind="box", x="species", y="bill_length_mm")
p.finalize(consolidate_legends=True)
```

👉 **Interactive Walkthrough:** [library/plotting.ipynb](library/plotting.ipynb)

<a id="syntax-conventions"></a>
## Syntax & Convention Cheat Sheet

| Task | Syntax | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Copy to Clipboard** | `df.to_clip()` in Python; `-o clip` in CLI | `df.head().to_clip()` |
| **Mapping vs. Assignment** | `:` maps old to new; `=` assigns values | `pt.replace_values(df, {"old": "new"})` vs `pt.mutate(col="expr")` |
| **Multi-Column (Mutate)** | Parentheses `(col1, col2)` + `_` placeholder | `df.pt.mutate("(rev, cost)_usd = _ * 1.08")` |
| **Spaced Columns (Filter)** | Enclose in brackets `[col]` | `df.pt.filter("[bill length mm] > 40")` |
| **Spaced Columns (Select)** | Enclose in brackets `[col]` | `df.pt.select("species", "[body mass g]")` |
| **Spaced Columns (Create)** | String assignment `[col] = ...` (or `**{...}`) | `df.pt.mutate("[body mass kg] = body_mass_g / 1000")` |
| **Spaced Columns (Agg)** | String mapping `"[col] = func, n = n"` | `df.pt.agg("smoker", "tip = mean, [total bill] = mean, n = n")` |
| **Spaced Columns (Expr)** | Reference via brackets `[col]` or backticks `` `col` `` | `df.pt.mutate(ratio="[bill length mm] / [bill depth mm]")` |
| **Standard Reshape Keys** | `c=` (column), `v=` (value), `a=` (aggregation) | `pt.wide(df, c="metric", v="value", a="mean")` |

# `agg` — Reference

[← Back to Library Reference Hub](../library.md)


`agg` aggregates numeric columns with grouping inherited from standalone `pt.by()` (or computes a whole-table summary when no grouping is set).

### Calling Styles

1. **Grouped aggregation**: `df.pt.by("species").pt.agg("mean")` or `df.pt.by("species").pt.agg(["sum", "mean", "n"])
2. **Keyword column mappings**: `df.pt.by("species").pt.agg(count="n", bill_length_mm="mean", body_mass_g=["sum", "mean"])
3. **Named output columns**: `df.pt.by("species").pt.agg(total="body_mass_g:sum")
4. **Whole-table summary**: `df.pt.agg("mean")` (computes grand totals across the entire table)

---

```python
import pytae as pt

penguins = pt.sample_data["penguins"]
tips = pt.sample_data["tips"]
titanic = pt.sample_data["titanic"]
penguins.head(3)
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |

## List `a` — `n` always goes first

```python
# mean + n: regardless of list order, n always comes first before aggregated columns
(
    penguins.pt.select("species", "island", "bill_length_mm", "body_mass_g")
    .pt.by("species", "island")
    .pt.agg(a=["mean", "n"])  # notice n comes first
)
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   n |   bill_length_mm |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|:----------|----:|-----------------:|--------------:|
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |  44 |          38.975  |       3709.66 |
| Adelie    | Dream     |  56 |          38.5018 |       3688.39 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |  52 |          38.951  |       3706.37 |
| Chinstrap | Dream     |  68 |          48.8338 |       3733.09 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe    | 124 |          47.5049 |       5076.02 |

```python
# Multiple numeric aggregations — column names get suffix: col_sum, col_mean, col_max
# also works with a single string if you only need one aggfunc
(penguins.pt.select("species", "bill_length_mm", "body_mass_g").pt.by("species").pt.agg(a=["sum", "mean", "max", "n"]))
```

**Output:**

| species   |   n |   bill_length_mm_sum |   bill_length_mm_mean |   bill_length_mm_max |   body_mass_g_sum |   body_mass_g_mean |   body_mass_g_max |
|:----------|----:|---------------------:|----------------------:|---------------------:|------------------:|-------------------:|------------------:|
| Adelie    | 152 |               5857.5 |               38.7914 |                 46   |            558800 |            3700.66 |              4775 |
| Chinstrap |  68 |               3320.7 |               48.8338 |                 58   |            253850 |            3733.09 |              4800 |
| Gentoo    | 124 |               5843.1 |               47.5049 |                 59.6 |            624350 |            5076.02 |              6300 |

## Keyword arguments — per-column control, output order follows parameter order

```python
# Keyword arguments — mean for bill_length, sum+mean for body_mass, count named 'n'
(
    penguins.pt.by("species").pt.agg(
        bill_length_mm="mean",
        body_mass_g=["sum", "mean"],
        n="n",
    )
)
```

**Output:**

| species   |   bill_length_mm |   body_mass_g_sum |   body_mass_g_mean |   n |
|:----------|-----------------:|------------------:|-------------------:|----:|
| Adelie    |          38.7914 |            558800 |            3700.66 | 152 |
| Chinstrap |          48.8338 |            253850 |            3733.09 |  68 |
| Gentoo    |          47.5049 |            624350 |            5076.02 | 124 |

```python
# Place count first (n at front), then aggregations
# Output order follows parameter order
# Note: the count keyword can be named anything — 'cnt', 'count', even 'maddy'
(
    tips.pt.select("smoker", "time", "total_bill", "tip")
    .pt.by("smoker", "time")
    .pt.agg(cnt="n", total_bill="mean", tip=["mean", "max"])
)
```

**Output:**

| smoker   | time   |   cnt |   total_bill |   tip_mean |   tip_max |
|:---------|:-------|------:|-------------:|-----------:|----------:|
| Yes      | Lunch  |    23 |      17.3991 |    2.83435 |       5   |
| Yes      | Dinner |    70 |      21.8594 |    3.066   |      10   |
| No       | Lunch  |    45 |      17.0509 |    2.67378 |       6.7 |
| No       | Dinner |   106 |      20.0957 |    3.12689 |       9   |

```python
# You can name the count column anything you like as a keyword argument
# Here maddy='n' creates a column called 'maddy' that holds the group count
(penguins.pt.select("species", "island", "body_mass_g").pt.by("species").pt.agg(maddy="n", body_mass_g="sum"))
```

**Output:**

| species   |   maddy |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|--------:|--------------:|
| Adelie    |     152 |        558800 |
| Chinstrap |      68 |        253850 |
| Gentoo    |     124 |        624350 |

```python
# Multiple count columns as keyword arguments — each count gets its own name
(
    penguins.pt.select("species", "island", "body_mass_g")
    .pt.by("species")
    .pt.agg(count="n", countv2="n", body_mass_g="mean")
)
```

**Output:**

| species   |   count |   countv2 |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|--------:|----------:|--------------:|
| Adelie    |     152 |       152 |       3700.66 |
| Chinstrap |      68 |        68 |       3733.09 |
| Gentoo    |     124 |       124 |       5076.02 |

```python
# median is a standard aggfunc — works in list form or as keyword argument
(
    penguins.pt.select("species", "island", "bill_length_mm", "body_mass_g")
    .pt.by("species")
    .pt.agg(a=["median", "mean", "n"])
)
```

**Output:**

| species   |   n |   bill_length_mm_median |   bill_length_mm_mean |   body_mass_g_median |   body_mass_g_mean |
|:----------|----:|------------------------:|----------------------:|---------------------:|-------------------:|
| Adelie    | 152 |                   38.8  |               38.7914 |                 3700 |            3700.66 |
| Chinstrap |  68 |                   49.55 |               48.8338 |                 3700 |            3733.09 |
| Gentoo    | 124 |                   47.3  |               47.5049 |                 5000 |            5076.02 |

## Handling Missing Group Keys (`dropna`)

```python
# Default dropna=False keeps missing grouping keys in their own group (no silent data loss)
(penguins.pt.select("species", "sex", "bill_length_mm", "body_mass_g").pt.by("species", "sex").pt.agg(a=["mean", "n"]))
```

```python
# Pass dropna=True to exclude groups with NaN keys
(
    penguins.pt.select("species", "sex", "bill_length_mm", "body_mass_g")
    .pt.by("species", "sex")
    .pt.agg(a=["mean", "n"], dropna=True)
```

## `n`-only aggregation — count with no numeric columns needed

```python
# Count only — useful for frequency tables on categorical columns
(penguins.pt.select(exclude_dtype="number").pt.by("species", "island").pt.agg(a="n"))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   n |
|:----------|:----------|----:|

| Chinstrap | Dream     |  68 |

## Pipeline Chaining: Filter -> Select -> Aggregation -> Sort

Because  operations return DataFrames, you can chain them seamlessly with standard Pandas operations:

```python
(
    penguins.pt.filter("body_mass_g > 3000")
    .pt.select("species", "sex", "body_mass_g")
    .pt.by("species", "sex")
    .pt.agg(a=["mean", "max", "n"])
    .sort_values("body_mass_g_mean", ascending=False)
)
```

**Output:**

| species   | sex    |   n |   body_mass_g_mean |   body_mass_g_max |
|:----------|:-------|----:|-------------------:|------------------:|
| Gentoo    | Male   |  61 |            5484.84 |              6300 |
| Gentoo    | Female |  58 |            4679.74 |              5200 |
| Gentoo    | nan    |   4 |            4587.5  |              4875 |
| Adelie    | Male   |  73 |            4043.49 |              4775 |
| Chinstrap | Male   |  34 |            3938.97 |              4800 |
| Adelie    | nan    |   4 |            3681.25 |              4250 |
| Chinstrap | Female |  32 |            3572.66 |              4150 |
| Adelie    | Female |  65 |            3424.62 |              3900 |

## Columns with Spaces & String Specifications

When column names have spaces, passing them as keyword arguments (`[total bill]='mean'`) is forbidden by Python syntax.

`agg` solves this by accepting **string mapping specifications** (matching the CLI `-agg` flag), where column names with spaces are enclosed in square brackets `[col]`. No dictionary unpacking `**{...}` is required:

```python
# Create DataFrame with spaced column names
tips_spaced = tips.rename(columns={"total_bill": "total bill"})

# Single string mapping with bracketed spaced columns
(tips_spaced.pt.by("smoker").pt.agg("tip = mean, [total bill] = mean, n = n"))
```

**Output:**

| smoker   |     tip |   total bill |   n |
|:---------|--------:|-------------:|----:|
| Yes      | 3.00871 |      20.7563 |  93 |
| No       | 2.99185 |      19.1883 | 151 |

```python
# Multiple positional string specifications
(tips_spaced.pt.by("smoker").pt.agg("tip = mean", "[total bill] = mean", "n = n"))
```

**Output:**

| smoker   |     tip |   total bill |   n |
|:---------|--------:|-------------:|----:|
| Yes      | 3.00871 |      20.7563 |  93 |
| No       | 2.99185 |      19.1883 | 151 |

```python
# Custom output names and bracketed source column
(tips_spaced.pt.by("smoker").pt.agg("[avg bill] = [total bill]:mean, [total tip] = tip:sum, [table count] = n"))
```

**Output:**

| smoker   |   avg bill |   total tip |   table count |
|:---------|-----------:|------------:|--------------:|
| Yes      |    20.7563 |      279.81 |            93 |
| No       |    19.1883 |      451.77 |           151 |

```python
# Complete pipeline: filter -> select -> agg with bracketed spaced columns across every verb
(
    tips.rename(columns={"total_bill": "total bill"})
    .pt.filter("[total bill] > 10", day=["Sat", "Sun"], time="Dinner", size=">= 2")
    .pt.select("smoker", "tip", "[total bill]")
    .pt.by("smoker")
    .pt.agg("tip = mean, [total bill] = mean, n = n")
)
```

**Output:**

| smoker   |     tip |   total bill |   n |
|:---------|--------:|-------------:|----:|
| Yes      | 3.08772 |      23.2323 |  57 |
| No       | 3.22546 |      20.7059 |  97 |

# `arrange` — Row Sorting & Ordering

[← Back to Library Reference Hub](../library.md)


`arrange` orders DataFrame rows by one or more columns with full support for descending orders (`desc`, `-col`), global `ascending=` overrides, and bracket notation for columns with spaces (`[col name]`).

| Method | Key Params | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `.pt.arrange(*cols, ascending=None, na_last=True)` | `*cols`, `ascending`, `na_last` | Sort rows ascending / descending |

---

```python
import pytae as pt

penguins = pt.sample_data["penguins"]
tips = pt.sample_data["tips"]
penguins.head(3)
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |

## 1. `arrange()` — Basic Sorting

By default, `.pt.arrange()` sorts in ascending order.

```python
# Sort ascending by body mass
(penguins.pt.arrange("body_mass_g").pt.select("species", "island", "body_mass_g").head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|:----------|--------------:|
| Chinstrap | Dream     |          2700 |
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |          2850 |
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |          2850 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          2900 |
| Adelie    | Dream     |          2900 |

## 2. Descending Order: `desc` keyword and `-` shorthand

Specify descending order either by appending `desc` or prefixing the column name with `-`.

```python
# Using explicit 'desc'
(penguins.pt.arrange("body_mass_g desc").pt.select("species", "island", "body_mass_g").head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island   |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|:---------|--------------:|
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          6300 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          6050 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          6000 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          6000 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          5950 |

```python
# Using leading minus '-' shorthand
(penguins.pt.arrange("-body_mass_g").pt.select("species", "island", "body_mass_g").head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island   |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|:---------|--------------:|
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          6300 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          6050 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          6000 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          6000 |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |          5950 |

## 3. Multi-Column Sorting

Pass multiple column specifications either as separate arguments or as a comma-separated string.

```python
# Multi-column: species ascending, body_mass_g descending
(penguins.pt.arrange("species", "body_mass_g desc").pt.select("species", "island", "body_mass_g").head(6))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|:----------|--------------:|
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |          4775 |
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |          4725 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          4700 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          4675 |
| Adelie    | Dream     |          4650 |
| Adelie    | Dream     |          4600 |

```python
# Comma-separated string with shorthand minus
(penguins.pt.arrange("species, -body_mass_g").pt.select("species", "island", "body_mass_g").head(6))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   body_mass_g |
|:----------|:----------|--------------:|
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |          4775 |
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |          4725 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          4700 |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          4675 |
| Adelie    | Dream     |          4650 |
| Adelie    | Dream     |          4600 |

## 4. Column Names with Spaces (`[col name]`)

Columns with spaces are cleanly referenced using square brackets `[col name]`.

```python
# Rename column to include spaces
spaced_penguins = penguins.rename(columns={"bill_length_mm": "bill length mm"})

# Sort by bracketed column name descending
(spaced_penguins.pt.arrange("[bill length mm] desc").pt.select("species", "[bill length mm]").head(5))
```

**Output:**

|:----------|-----------------:|
| Gentoo    |             59.6 |
| Chinstrap |             58   |
| Gentoo    |             55.9 |
| Chinstrap |             55.8 |
| Gentoo    |             55.1 |

## 5. Functional Style (`pt.arrange`)

Available as standalone functional verb `pt.arrange(df, ...)`:

```python
# Functional arrange
top_tips = pt.arrange(tips, "-tip")
top_tips[["total_bill", "tip", "day"]].head(4)
```

**Output:**

# FILE: docs/library/distinct.md

# Distinct Rows — Removing Duplicate Rows

[← Back to Library Reference Hub](../library.md)


Remove duplicate records across the intermediate DataFrame with full control over column subsets.

`pytae` provides both the method-chaining accessor `df.pt.distinct(*cols, keep='first')` and the functional verb `pt.distinct(df, *cols)`. In the CLI, the equivalent flag is `-distinct` (or `-distinct COLS`).

| Operation | Pytae Method Chain | CLI Equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| All Columns | `df.pt.distinct()` | `-distinct` |
| Specific Columns | `df.pt.distinct('col1', 'col2')` | `-distinct "col1,col2"` |
| Keep Last / None | `df.pt.distinct(keep='last')` | N/A |

---

```python
import pytae as pt
import pandas as pd

penguins = pt.sample_data["penguins"]
tips = pt.sample_data["tips"]
penguins.head(3)
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |

## 1. Deduplicating Across All Columns (`.pt.distinct()`)

Eliminate identical rows across all selected columns. The index is automatically reset:

```python
# Keep only unique species and island pairs
(penguins.pt.select("species", "island").pt.distinct())
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |
|:----------|:----------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |
| Adelie    | Dream     |
| Chinstrap | Dream     |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe    |

## 2. Deduplicating by Specific Identifier Columns

Pass column names to restrict duplicate checks to specific identifiers, keeping the first matching record for all other columns:

```python
# Keep the first recorded penguin for each unique species and island combination
(penguins.pt.select("species", "island", "body_mass_g", "sex").pt.distinct("species", "island"))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|:----------|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |          3400 | Female |
| Adelie    | Dream     |          3250 | Female |
| Chinstrap | Dream     |          3500 | Female |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe    |          4500 | Female |

## 3. Chaining in Pipelines

`df.pt.distinct()` flows seamlessly inside multi-step pipelines without dropping out of `.pt`:

```python
# Filter heavy penguins -> select columns -> deduplicate -> arrange
(penguins.pt.filter("body_mass_g > 4000").pt.select("species", "island").pt.distinct().pt.arrange("species", "island"))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |
|:----------|:----------|
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |
| Adelie    | Dream     |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |
| Chinstrap | Dream     |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe    |

## 4. Keeping the Last Record (`keep='last'`)

Optionally retain the last occurrence instead of the first:

```python
# Retain the last record for each day and time
(tips.pt.select("day", "time", "total_bill", "tip").pt.distinct("day", "time", keep="last"))
```

**Output:**

| day   | time   |   total_bill |   tip |
|:------|:-------|-------------:|------:|
| Fri   | Dinner |        15.38 |  3    |
| Sun   | Dinner |        15.69 |  1.5  |
| Thur  | Lunch  |        16.47 |  3.23 |
| Fri   | Lunch  |        10.09 |  2    |
| Sat   | Dinner |        17.82 |  1.75 |
| Thur  | Dinner |        18.78 |  3    |

## 5. Functional Style (`pt.distinct`)

Available as a standalone function:

```python
# Functional deduplication
pt.distinct(penguins[["species", "island"]])
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |
|:----------|:----------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |
| Adelie    | Biscoe    |
| Adelie    | Dream     |
| Chinstrap | Dream     |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe    |

# `filter` — Reference

[← Back to Library Reference Hub](../library.md)


`filter` filters a DataFrame using intuitive keyword arguments, CLI-style string expressions, plain dictionaries, or any combination of the three.

### Calling Styles

`filter` supports multiple flexible calling styles to fit interactive analysis, programmatic pipelines, and column names with spaces:

- **Keyword arguments**: `df.pt.filter(species='Adelie', body_mass_g='> 5000')`
- **String expressions** (matches CLI `-filter` syntax; handles spaces directly): `df.pt.filter("bill length mm > 40, species = 'Adelie'")`
- **Plain dictionaries** (ideal for dynamic keys or columns with spaces): `df.pt.filter({"bill length mm": "> 40", "species": "Adelie"})`
- **Mixed calling**: `df.pt.filter("bill length mm > 40", {"island": "Biscoe"}, species="Gentoo")`
- **Library function**: `pt.filter(df, species='Adelie', body_mass_g='> 5000')`

### Supported Condition Types

| Condition | Example Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Equality | `species='Adelie'` or `"species = Adelie"` | exact match |
| Membership | `species=['Adelie', 'Gentoo']` | in list |
| Tuple membership | `species=('in', ['Adelie', 'Gentoo'])` | in list |
| Exclusion | `sex=('not in', ['Male'])` | not in list |
| Comparison (operator) | `body_mass_g='> 5000'` or `body_mass_g=('>', 5000)` | `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `==`, `!=` |
| Open interval | `body_mass_g='(3500,4500)'` | `3500 < x < 4500` |
| Half-open interval | `bill_length_mm='[40,50)'` | `40 <= x < 50` |
| Closed interval | `body_mass_g='[3500,4000]'` | `3500 <= x <= 4000` |
| String matching | `species=('startswith', 'Ad')` | `startswith`, `endswith`, `contains`, `regex` |
| Multiple prefixes/suffixes | `species=('startswith', ['Ad', 'Ge'])` | matches any prefix/suffix in list/tuple |
| Null check | `sex=('isna',)` / `sex=('notna',)` | missing / non-missing (unary tuple) |
| Columns with spaces | `"bill length mm > 40"` or `{"bill length mm": "> 40"}` | spaces handled without dict unpacking |
| Same-column bounds | `"mass > 3000, mass < 5000"` or `"mass > 3000", "mass < 5000"` | multiple conditions on same column |

---

```python
import pytae as pt

penguins = pt.sample_data["penguins"]
tips = pt.sample_data["tips"]
titanic = pt.sample_data["titanic"]
penguins.head(3)
```

**Output:**

| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |

## Flexible calling styles: kwargs, string expressions, and dictionaries

`filter()` accepts conditions as keyword arguments, string expressions matching the CLI `-filter` syntax, plain dictionaries, or any mix of the three. Both the DataFrame accessor (`df.pt.filter(...)`) and the top-level library verb (`pt.filter(df, ...)`) are supported.

```python

(penguins.pt.filter(species="Adelie", island="Dream").head(5))
```

| Adelie    | Dream    |             39.5 |            17.8 |                 188 |          3300 | Female |
| Adelie    | Dream    |             40.9 |            18.9 |                 184 |          3900 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Dream    |             36.4 |            17   |                 195 |          3325 | Female |

```python
# 2. String expressions — matches pytae CLI -qry syntax; supports comma-separated conditions
(penguins.pt.filter("species = 'Adelie', body_mass_g > 4000").head(5))
```

|:----------|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.2 |            19.6 |                 195 |          4675 | Male  |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             42   |            20.2 |                 190 |          4250 | nan   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             34.6 |            21.1 |                 198 |          4400 | Male  |

```python
# 3. Plain dictionaries — useful for programmatic pipelines or dynamic key mapping
(penguins.pt.filter({"species": "Adelie", "island": "Dream"}).head(5))
```

## Column names with spaces — bracket notation `[col]`

When columns have spaces (like `'bill length mm'`), enclose them in square brackets `[col]` inside string expressions. This avoids keyword argument restrictions and dictionary unpacking entirely.

```python
# DataFrame with spaces in column names
penguins_spaces = penguins.rename(columns={"bill_length_mm": "bill length mm", "body_mass_g": "body mass g"})

# String expressions with brackets handle spaced column names cleanly:
(penguins_spaces.pt.filter("[bill length mm] > 45", "[body mass g] > 4000").head(5))
```

## Comparison operators

Comparison filters can be written as string expressions (`body_mass_g="> 5000"`) or operator tuples (`body_mass_g=('>', 5000)`).
Supported comparison operators: `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`.

```python
# Filter penguins with body mass greater than 5000g (string operator)
(penguins.pt.filter(body_mass_g="> 5000").head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island   |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex   |

| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |             50   |            16.3 |                 230 |          5700 | Male  |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |             50   |            15.2 |                 218 |          5700 | Male  |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |             47.6 |            14.5 |                 215 |          5400 | Male  |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |             46.7 |            15.3 |                 219 |          5200 | Male  |
| Gentoo    | Biscoe   |             46.8 |            15.4 |                 215 |          5150 | Male  |

```python
# Tuple operator syntax: ('>', 5000)
(penguins.pt.filter(body_mass_g=(">", 5000)).head(5))
```

## Interval notation
String intervals let you filter a range on the same column without chaining two `.pt.filter()` calls.
`(` / `)` = exclusive bound, `[` / `]` = inclusive bound.

```python
# Open interval — strictly between 3500 and 4500 g via kwargs:
(penguins.pt.filter(body_mass_g="(3500,4500)").head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |

| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.3 |            20.6 |                 190 |          3650 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             38.9 |            17.8 |                 181 |          3625 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             42   |            20.2 |                 190 |          4250 | nan    |

```python
# Half-open interval — bill_length_mm >= 40 and < 50
(penguins.pt.filter(bill_length_mm="[40,50)").head(5))
```

| Adelie    | Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |

| Adelie    | Torgersen |             41.1 |            17.6 |                 182 |          3200 | Female |

| Adelie    | Torgersen |             46   |            21.5 |                 194 |          4200 | Male   |

```python
# Closed interval — body_mass_g between 3500 and 4000 inclusive
(penguins.pt.filter(body_mass_g="[3500,4000]").head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.3 |            20.6 |                 190 |          3650 | Male   |

| Adelie    | Torgersen |             37.8 |            17.3 |                 180 |          3700 | nan    |

```python
# Interval notation also works on STRING columns — alphabetical comparison
# 'island' values: Biscoe, Dream, Torgersen — (Biscoe, Dream] means Dream only
(penguins.pt.filter(island="(Biscoe,Dream]").sample())
```

|:----------|:---------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Dream    |             37.6 |            19.3 |                 181 |          3300 | Female |

## String matching and null checks
`startswith`/`endswith`/`contains`/`regex` use pandas' `.str` accessor (missing values never match, `na=False`). `contains`/`regex` both search anywhere in the string (like `re.search`) — `regex` is just `contains` with `regex=True`.

`startswith` and `endswith` also accept a list or tuple of multiple prefixes/suffixes. `isna`/`notna` are one-element tuples since they take no value.

```python
# species starting with 'Ad' — same idea for endswith/contains
(penguins.pt.filter(species=("startswith", "Ad")).head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.1 |            18.7 |                 181 |          3750 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             39.5 |            17.4 |                 186 |          3800 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |            nan   |           nan   |                 nan |           nan | nan    |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             36.7 |            19.3 |                 193 |          3450 | Female |

```python
# Multiple prefixes: species starting with 'Ad' OR 'Ge'
(penguins.pt.filter(species=("startswith", ["Ad", "Ge"])).head(5))
```

**Output:**

## Multiple conditions on the same column

Because Python keyword arguments must have unique names, you cannot pass `bill_length_mm='> 40', bill_length_mm='< 50'` in kwargs. With `filter()`, you have multiple intuitive solutions:

1. **Comma-separated string expression**: `"bill_length_mm > 40, bill_length_mm < 50"`
2. **Multiple positional string arguments**: `"bill_length_mm > 40", "bill_length_mm < 50"`
3. **Interval notation**: `bill_length_mm='[40,50)'`
4. **Chained `.pt.filter()` calls**: `.pt.filter(bill_length_mm='> 40').pt.filter(bill_length_mm='< 50')`

```python
# Comma-separated string expression on the same column:
(penguins.pt.filter("bill_length_mm > 40, bill_length_mm < 50").head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |
|:----------|:----------|-----------------:|----------------:|--------------------:|--------------:|:-------|
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             40.3 |            18   |                 195 |          3250 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             42   |            20.2 |                 190 |          4250 | nan    |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             41.1 |            17.6 |                 182 |          3200 | Female |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             42.5 |            20.7 |                 197 |          4500 | Male   |
| Adelie    | Torgersen |             46   |            21.5 |                 194 |          4200 | Male   |

```python
# Multiple string arguments:
(penguins.pt.filter("bill_length_mm > 40", "bill_length_mm < 50").head(5))
```

**Output:**

| species   | island    |   bill_length_mm |   bill_depth_mm |   flipper_length_mm |   body_mass_g | sex    |

```python
# Chaining two .pt.filter() calls:
```

## Helpful typo suggestions

If a column name is misspelled, `filter()` suggests close matches using fuzzy matching to help catch typos immediately.

```python
# Intentional typo 'speceis' raises KeyError with a helpful suggestion
try:
    penguins.pt.filter(speceis="Adelie")
except KeyError as exc:
    print("Caught expected error:", exc)
```

**Output:**
```text
Caught expected error: "unknown column 'speceis' (did you mean 'species'?)"
```

## Real-world pipeline: filter → aggregate

```python
# Tips: weekend dinner table of 2+, spending > $10 — average tip and bill by smoker status
# Using bracket notation [total bill] across qry and agg:
(
    tips.rename(columns={"total_bill": "total bill"})
    .pt.filter("[total bill] > 10", day=["Sat", "Sun"], time="Dinner", size=">= 2")
    .pt.by("smoker")
    .pt.agg("tip = mean, [total bill] = mean, n = n")
)
```

**Output:**

| smoker   |     tip |   total bill |   n |
|:---------|--------:|-------------:|----:|
| Yes      | 3.08772 |      23.2323 |  57 |
| No       | 3.22546 |      20.7059 |  97 |

# Data Input & Output (I/O) — Ingestion, Streaming, and Sinks

`pytae` provides a unified, high-throughput I/O engine powered by a 100% native multithreaded SIMD Polars core with seamless Apache Arrow memory layouts.

This guide covers:
- **Eager Reading (`pt.read`)**: Fast, immediate in-memory loading.
- **Lazy Scanning (`pt.scan`)**: Query pushdown, projection pruning, and predicate skipping.
- **Dual-Mode Execution**: Writing fluent pipelines without manual `.collect()` juggling.
- **Universal Constructor (`pt.DataFrame`)**: Seamless interop across Polars, Pandas, Arrow, and Python dictionaries.
- **Writing Data (Sinks)**: Out-of-core streaming exports (`to_parquet`, `to_csv`, `to_pandas`, `to_clip`).
- **Bundled Datasets & Sampling**: `pt.sample()` and random row sampling.

<a id="eager-vs-lazy"></a>
## Eager Ingestion (`pt.read`) vs. Lazy Evaluation (`pt.scan`)

Traditional data science tools (such as standard Pandas `pd.read_csv` or `pd.read_parquet`) read datasets **eagerly**, loading every row and column into RAM before any filtering or column selection can begin. On larger-than-RAM or multi-gigabyte datasets, this produces excessive I/O wait times and Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes.

Pytae provides two complementary paradigms:

```
                    ┌────────────────────────┐
                    │      Source File       │
                    │ (.parquet, .csv, etc.) │
                    └───────────┬────────────┘
                                │
             ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐
             ▼                                     ▼
     Eager Ingestion                        Lazy Evaluation
      pt.read(path)                         pt.scan(path)
             │                                     │
             ▼                                     ▼
   Materializes to RAM                     Builds Query Graph
   • Polars SIMD Reader                    • Projection Pushdown
   • Immediate row access                  • Predicate Pushdown
   • In-memory DataFrame                   • Slice Pushdown
                                                   │
                                                   ▼
                                         Single .collect()
                                         Only reads what's needed!
```

---

<a id="eager-reading"></a>
## Eager Reading (`pt.read`)

`pt.read()` reads data off disk immediately into a `pytae.DataFrame` backed by a native Polars `DataFrame`. It automatically infers the file format from the file extension.

```python
import pytae as pt

# Direct reading from Parquet
df = pt.read("transactions.parquet")

# Direct reading from CSV
df_csv = pt.read("customers.csv")
```

### Supported File Formats

| Format | Extension | Underlying Engine | Auto-Detected Defaults |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Parquet** | `.parquet`, `.pq` | Native Polars SIMD Parquet | Snappy, ZSTD, Gzip compression |
| **CSV** | `.csv` | Native Polars Fast CSV | Comma-separated (`,`), UTF-8 |
| **TSV / Tab Text** | `.tsv`, `.txt` | Native Polars Fast CSV | Tab-separated (`\t`) |
| **DAT / Pipe Text**| `.dat` | Native Polars Fast CSV | Pipe-separated (`\|`), Latin-1 |
| **Line JSON** | `.jsonl`, `.ndjson` | Native Polars NDJSON | Newline-delimited JSON records |
| **Excel** | `.xlsx`, `.xls` | Calamine / OpenXML | Primary worksheet |
| **Compressed** | `.csv.gz`, `.txt.gz`, `.dat.gz`, `.ndjson.gz` | Native Gzip Stream | Auto-decompression on read |

### Custom Delimiters & Encodings

Any additional keyword arguments passed to `pt.read()` are forwarded directly to the underlying Polars reader:

```python
# Custom delimiter and encoding
df = pt.read("data.csv", separator=";", encoding="latin-1")

# Read specific columns only
df = pt.read("data.parquet", columns=["user_id", "total_amount"])

# Limit rows read into memory
df = pt.read("huge_data.csv", n_rows=1000)
```

### Remote URLs & Compressed Files

`pt.read()` natively accepts HTTP and HTTPS URLs and compressed archives:

```python
# Read directly from public HTTPS URL
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mwaskom/seaborn-data/master/penguins.csv"
penguins = pt.read(url)

# Read directly from gzipped CSV
logs = pt.read("access_logs.csv.gz")
```

---

<a id="lazy-scanning"></a>
## Lazy Scanning & Query Pushdowns (`pt.scan`)

`pt.scan()` registers the dataset into Polars' query planner without loading row data into RAM. It returns a `pytae.DataFrame` with `is_lazy == True` wrapping a `polars.LazyFrame`.

```python
import pytae as pt

# Instant scan: reads only header/schema metadata (0 rows in RAM!)
lazy_df = pt.scan("massive_sales.parquet")

# Build a fluent analytical pipeline
query = (
    lazy_df.pt.select("region", "store_id", "revenue", "order_date")
    .pt.filter("revenue > 500.0 and region == 'West'")
    .pt.by("region", "store_id")
    .pt.agg(total_rev="sum(revenue)", num_orders="n")
    .pt.arrange("total_rev", ascending=False)
    .pt.head(10)
)

# Materialize execution: executes the fully optimized query plan
top_stores = query.collect()
```

### Hardware Query Optimizations

When using `pt.scan()`, the Polars query optimizer reorganizes operations to minimize hardware disk I/O, CPU decompression cycles, and RAM consumption.

```
Parquet on Disk (100 Columns, 50,000,000 Rows across 100 Row Groups)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [Row Group 1] min(amount)=10, max(amount)=250   ──► SKIPPED (Predicate Pushdown)
│ [Row Group 2] min(amount)=150, max(amount)=8000 ──► READ ONLY col 'amount' & 'id'
│ [Row Group 3] min(amount)=5, max(amount)=90    ──► SKIPPED (Predicate Pushdown)
│ ...                                                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 1. Projection Pushdown (Column Pruning)
If a table has 80 columns but your pipeline only references `user_id` and `amount`:
- **Standard Pandas**: Reads all 80 columns from disk, allocates memory for all 80, and drops 78 columns in memory.
- **Pytae / Polars**: Passes the column projection down to the reader. **Only the 2 requested columns are read off disk.** The remaining 78 columns are never read, decompressed, or allocated in RAM.

#### 2. Predicate Pushdown (Row-Group Skipping)
If your pipeline filters `.pt.filter("amount > 1000")`:
- Parquet files contain metadata headers with `min` and `max` statistics for each column within each row group (~100,000 rows per group).
- Pytae evaluates the filter predicate against the row group statistics **before reading**.
- Any row group where `max(amount) <= 1000` is **completely skipped**. The disk read heads never touch those blocks, and zero decompression CPU cycles are consumed.

#### 3. Slice Pushdown (Early Termination)
If your pipeline ends with `.head(5)`:
- The file reader terminates reading as soon as 5 matching rows are obtained, rather than reading the entire file and discarding the rest.

<a id="read-vs-scan-performance"></a>
### Performance Comparison: When to Use Read vs. Scan

| Scenario | Recommended API | Why? |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| **Selective Query on Large File** (filtering rows or selecting specific columns) | `pt.scan()` | **10x–50x faster**: Projection and predicate pushdowns avoid reading 90%+ of the file off disk. |
| **Quick Peek at Large File** (`.head(5)`) | `pt.scan()` | **Instant (~0.003s)**: Slice pushdown terminates reading after the first batch. |
| **Full Ingestion of Entire CSV** (all columns, all rows, no filtering) | `pt.read()` | **Faster than `scan().collect()`**: Eager parser reads contiguous bytes into Arrow memory without streaming query-engine chunk coordination. |
| **Small to Medium Datasets (< 500 MB)** | `pt.read()` | Simpler immediate row access without query planning overhead. |

---

<a id="dual-mode-execution"></a>
## Dual-Mode Execution: Best of Both Without `.collect()`

In native Polars, `pl.DataFrame` and `pl.LazyFrame` are two separate classes with distinct APIs. Users must constantly remember when to call `.lazy()` and when to call `.collect()`.

In `pytae`, **both eager and lazy tables are wrapped in the universal `pytae.DataFrame` container**:
- Every fluent verb (`.select()`, `.filter()`, `.mutate()`, `.arrange()`, `.dropna()`, `.by()`, `.agg()`) works identically on both eager and lazy data.
- If you start with `pt.scan()`, operations chain invisibly as a lazy query graph.

<a id="zero-cost-metadata"></a>
### Zero-Cost Schema & Metadata Inspection
On a lazy dataset, inspecting metadata does not trigger a slow, full table scan:
- **`df.columns`**: Calls `collect_schema().names()`. Resolves column names directly from schema metadata with **0 rows read**.
- **`df.dtypes` / `df.schema`**: Calls `collect_schema()`. Returns Arrow type definitions without parsing table data.
- **`df.shape` & `len(df)`**: Evaluates `_df.select(pl.len()).collect().item()`. Polars computes the exact row count in $\sim 0.01\text{ s}$ (often directly from Parquet metadata footers) without allocating column memory in RAM.

<a id="just-in-time"></a>
### Just-In-Time Materialization
Pytae materializes data **just-in-time** when external libraries or output sinks require concrete values:

| Action / Method | What Happens Behind the Scenes |
|:---|:---|
| `df.to_pandas()` | Collects the lazy plan and returns a Pandas DataFrame with original indices preserved. |
| `df.plot(...)` | Collects the analytical result and passes it to the Matplotlib Plotter. |
| `df.to_clip()` | Collects the TSV stream and copies to the OS clipboard (`pbcopy`, `clip`, `xclip`). |
| `df.values` / `to_numpy()` | Materializes the minimum required columns to a NumPy ndarray. |
| `df.head(5)` | Slices the lazy plan with `.head(5)` and pushes the early termination limit down to the reader. |

---

<a id="universal-constructor"></a>
## Universal Constructor (`pt.DataFrame`)

`pt.DataFrame(data)` creates a Pytae DataFrame from almost any tabular data structure:

```python
import pytae as pt
import polars as pl
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

# 1. From an existing Polars DataFrame or LazyFrame (Zero-copy wrapper)
pldf = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]})
df1 = pt.DataFrame(pldf)

# 2. From a Pandas DataFrame (Seamless Arrow conversion, original index preserved)
pdf = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Alice", "Bob"], "age": [25, 30]}, index=["row1", "row2"])
df2 = pt.DataFrame(pdf)

# 3. From a PyArrow Table
arrow_tbl = pa.table({"x": [1, 2], "y": ["a", "b"]})
df3 = pt.DataFrame(arrow_tbl)

# 4. From raw Python dicts or records
df4 = pt.DataFrame({"id": [101, 102], "status": ["active", "pending"]})
```

---

<a id="data-output"></a>
## Data Output & Export Sinks

Pytae provides high-performance output sinks for saving, converting, or copying transformed tables.

<a id="to-parquet"></a>
### Streaming Parquet Export (`to_parquet`)

When writing transformed data to Parquet:
```python
df.to_parquet("output.parquet")
```
- **On eager DataFrames**: Writes directly via multithreaded SIMD Arrow serialization.
- **On lazy DataFrames**: Automatically attempts Polars' out-of-core streaming engine (**`sink_parquet()`**). Data streams directly from the source disk through your pipeline into the destination file. You can transform a **100 GB dataset on an 8 GB laptop** without running out of RAM!

<a id="to-csv"></a>
### Streaming CSV Export (`to_csv`)

```python
df.to_csv("output.csv")
```
- Automatically attempts streaming **`sink_csv()`** on lazy plans.
- Respects custom separators: `df.to_csv("output.tsv", separator="\t")`.

<a id="interop"></a>
### Pandas & Polars Interoperability

```python
# Convert to Pandas DataFrame (original indices and column types preserved)
pdf = df.to_pandas()

# Extract the underlying Polars DataFrame (collecting if lazy)
pldf = df.to_polars()
```

<a id="to-clip"></a>
### System Clipboard Export (`to_clip`)

Quickly paste analytical results into Slack, Excel, or Google Sheets:
```python
# Copies the table to clipboard as clean TSV (without row index numbers)
df.to_clip()
```
Works across macOS (`pbcopy`), Windows (`clip`), and Linux (`xclip`).
